item.title: The French Fantasy Is Coming to an End
item.description:
On Saturday, protests shut down large swaths of Paris. In parts of the city and around the country, pockets of these demonstrations turned violent. Looting and arson marked streets near Place de la République and in the First Arrondissement, where shop windows were broken and electric bikes were set on fire. In the city of Limoges, the 19th-century Hôtel de Ville went up in flames; in Lyon, a tourist office blazed.

Protests here began in late September with students in the suburbs exhausted by the conditions of their schools, including their inability to cool or heat classrooms, keep out rats or simply keep teachers. This weekend, hundreds of thousands of French men and women joined the students on the streets in an expression of mass frustration over the cost of living, extreme wealth disparity, government paralysis and a faltering social welfare system.

For the past decade, I have spent part of every year in Paris. Protests are a fact of life here, but Saturday’s were different, larger, more intense. Many groups, including the Gilets Jaunes (Yellow Vests) — a protest movement that seized the country in 2018 and 2019 over the falling quality of life — joined the students, along with labor unions.

I left the Left Bank and set out on foot for the Bastille, 30 minutes away across the Seine, on Saturday around noon. The Bastille column was covered in graffiti from a demonstration the previous week. There I caught the tail end of a procession of people making their way toward Place de la République. It was a largely peaceful group of mostly young people, some holding signs mocking President Emmanuel Macron, some waving French flags. Intermittently, marchers would break out in chanting and clapping.

At République, police officers ringed the square, dressed in riot gear as though preparing to go to war. It was crowded but civil. Some people wore surgical masks, others gas masks, ready for tear gas, the faint smell of which was already in the air. Television crews interviewed protesters. A few climbed the statue of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, and waved French flags. Shortly after I arrived, flash bangs began going off on one of the side streets toward Canal St. Martin, and canisters of tear gas could be seen sailing through the air. Crowds began running back into the square. As the tear gas grew thicker, I sought a quick exit down the narrow path the police had provided for people to leave.

It was only on Sunday that I saw the shattered windows, looted stores and charred remains of electric bikes.

The violence of the protests, which was amplified on social media and apparently the result of rioters exploiting the moment, threatens to undermine the message of the students and risks resulting in the exact opposite of their goals, which is to petition for more government resources devoted to education and, by extension, a more sustainable future.

These days of protest and rage have struck me as more than just a rebuff to the French government. The students’ fury is giving voice to some larger social failures many of us, in France and elsewhere, often fail to face directly: the climate catastrophe, the terror of artificial intelligence, the faltering economic picture. The students’ determination to voice their anger and frustration over the future is a necessary and courageous reminder that we all need to be facing facts and acting on them.

On my bike ride home from République on Saturday, I encountered an impromptu gathering of students singing “La Marseillaise,” the French national anthem. As they passed the intersection, some set down bikes and other objects to block cars and make the trip more difficult for everyone. That’s as it should be, I thought, as I navigated past the makeshift barricades. Against the backdrop of so many destructive forces, none of us, anywhere, should be allowed to proceed easily.

Since late spring, a series of calamities, in quick succession, have taken a battering ram to the fantasy that Paris is some sort of respite from the problems plaguing the world. A number of punishing, record-breaking heat waves roiled the country, beginning in May. Temperatures in Paris soared above 100 degrees Fahrenheit again and again this summer. Joyful images of young Parisians leaping into the Canal St. Martin and the Seine were sobered by a national death toll of nearly 8,000 and fires that burned tens of thousands of acres. The spectacle of haute couture shows held in the extreme heat felt especially grotesque. Walking through the city this fall, I still see the tattered remains of silver foil hacked together to keep out the heat fluttering from windows. Every piece of store-bought chocolate I’ve purchased since summer is white from having melted and resolidified. As October began, I wandered into the Pride parade rescheduled after the extreme heat made it untenable.

And then the streets were aflame.

All this is happening against the impending presidential election next spring, which currently favors the far-right candidate Marine Le Pen. To paraphrase F. Scott Fitzgerald, chronicler of the interwar period (another era known for its wild abandon), a restlessness approaches hysteria, with menacing undertones that have finally burst to the fore with the protests. Mr. Macron, the target of much of the students’ anger and derision, didn’t help matters much by spending his Friday night with Celine Dion, dancing at the city’s most coveted concert just before parts of Paris burned.

In a speech broadcast live Sunday night, Mr. Macron made a point to differentiate between the protesters’ “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed and looted.” He said, “We all feel anger and shame.”

Americans, in particular, have always been susceptible to the country’s siren call. Last year, France had a 14 percent increase in first-time residency permits issued to Americans. As life and politics in the United States have grown ever harsher and more punishing, Americans have craved France’s monthlong vacations and universal health care (if not the tax burden that supports them).

But now, with Saturday’s enormous — and enormously destructive — protests, the dream that there is a place of escape may be nearing an end. With their anger and determination to tap into France’s long history of revolution, students are showing the rest of the world that the only way to march into the dark future is together.

Loudly. And with cleareyed resolve. Their challenge now is to keep the violence at bay. If there is a French fantasy to pursue in these tumultuous times, this must be the one.

Glynnis MacNicol is a contributing Opinion writer. She is the author of “I’m Mostly Here to Enjoy Myself.”

item.title: The Unrelenting Nightmare of Applying to High School in New York City
item.description:
Until recently, I thought my worst New York City experience was the time I was waiting to cross Houston Street and a cackling vagrant punched me in the face. That, however, was before I started the process of getting my oldest kid into a public high school.

New York has an almost purely school choice system; most families don’t have a default high school that they’re zoned for. The admissions process, a mix of meritocratic culling and sheer chance, is time-consuming, psychologically taxing and so byzantine that it’s hard to describe to anyone who hasn’t endured it.

“I was somehow holding it together with all the balls in the air until this high school process,” Eva Pinkley, a single mother in Brooklyn, told me last week, as her neurodivergent son worked on an application essay with a coach she could barely afford. Now, she said, “I’m completely falling apart.” An education reporter I know contemplated moving out of the city after seeing high school applications up close. Friends of mine who’ve endured the process say the only consolation is that it makes applying to college seem easy.

I’d heard how miserable it was before it was my turn, but was still shocked by it, in part because of a stroke of particularly bad luck. My kid will, I think, be fine — I will go to great lengths to assure it — but I’m not sure how people with fewer resources cope. And the whole nightmare made me curious about how it got this way, and who all this punishing complexity serves.

“By many measures, New York is the kind of city where school choice is supposed to shine,” writes the Princeton sociologist Jennifer L. Jennings in her recent book about school choice, “The Scarcity Loop.” It’s huge and wealthy, with hundreds of options and good public transportation. But the problem in New York, as in most other big cities, is that there aren’t enough seats in excellent schools to go around.

So getting into high school feels like playing multiple games of musical chairs simultaneously. Places are distributed according to a bewildering mixture of lotteries, grades, tests, interviews, essays, auditions and portfolios. School choice is meant to be fairer than rationing education by ZIP code — as typically happens in suburbs — and in some ways it is. But the system in New York is a bureaucratic Rube Goldberg machine that locks out families that don’t know how to operate it while driving privileged ones crazy. It demonstrates the way school choice policies can shift responsibility for securing each kid a great education away from government and onto individuals. They trap us in a joyless competition and make us feel like it’s our fault when we lose.

“Families with institutional fluency and flexible schedules are better equipped to manage this hidden curriculum,” Jennings writes in “The Scarcity Loop.” “Others, facing language barriers or inflexible work, are filtered out by the grind itself, excluded by process rather than lines on a map. Even for savvy parents, the process leaves its mark in the erosion of evenings, weekends and mothers’ sleep.”

On New York’s high school application, families list the schools they’re applying to in order of preference. Students are divided up into five tiers based on their marks in seventh grade, and, separately, assigned a hexadecimal lottery number — really a combination of letters and numbers — that determines their priority in the city’s school-matching algorithm. (The meaning of the lottery numbers is indecipherable to laypeople, but parents in the know turn to a chart created by the computer science professor Amélie Marian, a revered figure on the school-application message boards.) Some schools take kids only from the highest tier, which can shut out those who get a single A- in seventh grade. But perfect grades are no guarantee, either, if you get a bad lottery number.

This year my son was in the top tier, but Marian’s data showed that his lottery number was among the worst possible. That means we’ll be matched to a school only after the other 99 percent of city kids are given their choices of the schools they qualify for. By then, the schools that usually take kids only from the top tier are expected to be full. So will the most desirable schools that accept kids from across the academic spectrum.

We’re hanging our hopes on the SHSAT, an SAT-like test that determines access to eight of the city’s specialized high schools, as well as a handful of other public schools with their own tests, essays and interviews. And while I respect arguments against the charter school movement — I even agree with some of them — we’ve applied to a well-regarded Brooklyn charter school and I have found myself wishing there were more.

Since none of these options are sure bets, we’re seeking out safety schools that are well run but not too selective, reasonably rigorous and, importantly, no more than an hour away by public transportation. To find them, we’ve relied on social media, word of mouth — parents we know have assembled spreadsheets — and a Zoom meeting with an embarrassingly expensive consultant. Having come up with a handful of backup schools, we’re trying to visit them during tours and open houses, though often these fill up so quickly that parents trade spots online.

Obviously, the lottery system isn’t unfair just because we got the short end of it; someone has to be last. What infuriates me is the underlying shortage of seats in schools that are challenging and well resourced, forcing parents to scratch and claw for a place, or to settle. The system creates a sense that “if it fails, it’s on you,” Jennings told me. “If you jump through the right hoops and know the secret codes at the right time, you’ll be able to get a seat.”

There’s no way to know how many families are driven out of the public school system by this ordeal. But we do know that enrollment in New York’s public schools is shrinking. In an Education Department survey released last year, 41 percent of families that withdrew from the city’s public school system said they were seeking “more rigorous” education. Forty percent departed because their families moved. Among that group, half said “concerns about schools” were one of their reasons for leaving the city. It seems obvious that the “Hunger Games” aspect of public high school admissions is a drag on New York’s fortunes, one Zohran Mamdani needs to address, though he didn’t create it.

Some of the system’s maddening features date back to Michael Bloomberg’s administration. Bloomberg closed underperforming neighborhood schools and encouraged the proliferation of small, career-focused high schools. Today, the city has lots of themed schools — there are schools for sports management, marketing and hip-hop — but not nearly enough neighborhood high schools with broad, general-interest offerings and honors tracks. Without a zoned high school, families have little incentive to lobby to make their local ones better. Ambitious kids often must resign themselves to long commutes. “High-achieving kids travel a lot farther than lower-achieving kids,” said Jennings.

Public school inequality is a wicked problem, and I won’t pretend to have an easy solution to it. Ultimately, I think part of the answer is bringing back neighborhood high schools, not as a replacement for school choice, but as a supplement. “The process is extremely stress-inducing because people feel that they don’t have agency and they don’t have predictability,” said Marian, the computer scientist. If all parents had at least one community school they could depend on, some predictability would be restored.

But that’s a long-term goal. In the short term, Mamdani’s administration, so focused on making government more responsive to its citizens, can look for ways to take some of the pain out of the application process. Here’s one small idea:

Several of the most sought-after schools ask students to submit essays about how they will both contribute to and benefit from those schools’ unique pedagogical approaches. In a system in which families are scrambling for any foothold they can find, these assignments do not encourage sincerity. They are unrewarding to write and tedious to oversee. If schools want a writing component, there should be one essay, maybe with a choice of prompts, used for all of them.

Overall, the goal should be more ease and simplicity. “Rationing always imposes work somewhere; the moral question is where that work lands, and who pays,” writes Jennings. Right now, most of the work falls on parents. The one resource this system treats as inexhaustible is families’ time.

item.title: Amish Families Pushed to Undo a Vaccine Law. Then Measles Arrived.
item.description:
For five years, the New York State Health Department has been locked in battle with three tiny Amish schools upstate. The dispute: whether students must be vaccinated.

Amish families say that New York’s immunization rules, which allow no religious exemptions, threaten their religious freedom and way of life. The state insists that unvaccinated children — which would include most of the students at the three schools — must be barred from the classroom.

In a petition filed on Sept. 28, the Amish asked the U.S. Supreme Court to force New York to grant religious exemptions to immunization rules, as most states do. A previous ruling gave the Amish reason to think they might have a chance at prevailing.

But then a wave of measles cases began sweeping through Amish communities. Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide health emergency this month after more than 100 people fell ill with measles.

“Perhaps Mother Nature, by delivering a measles outbreak in New York’s Amish community coincident with this case returning to the Supreme Court, is her not-so-subtle hint,” said Dr. Howard Zucker, who was state health commissioner when New York eliminated religious exemptions.

But many Amish families regard vaccine mandates — and government intrusion in their schools — as a greater threat to the health of their community than measles. Their religion calls for adherents to live together in tightknit religious communities apart from the modern world and its influences.

“Our almighty God wants us to fully put our faith and trust in him, which is in conflict to put our trust in vaccines,” Ezra Wengerd, an Amish leader who represents the 26 families that send their children to the three schools, told a judge in 2022.

Measles is on the rise across the United States. More than 4,400 cases have been reported this year. The Amish have been hard hit, although they are far from the only group affected.

The clusters of cases in New York appear linked to larger outbreaks in Amish communities in Ohio and Pennsylvania.

In New York, most of the cases upstate appear to have been in Amish and Mennonite communities, according to interviews and local news accounts. Health officials have been reluctant to say so outright, they acknowledged, for fear of stigmatizing those communities.

“It’s in rural New York — that’s what’s important,” Dr. James McDonald, the state health commissioner, said in a recent interview.

One county health official, Dr. Kevin Watkins of Cattaraugus County, confirmed during a county health board meeting that most cases in upstate New York were clustered “within Plain communities,” a name used to describe Amish and Mennonite groups that emphasizes the unadorned nature of their clothing and lifestyle.

More than 20,000 Amish residents live across upstate New York, from the westernmost corner to the North Country region. Signs of the outbreak are not tough to find.

In Chautauqua County, in Western New York, one man said that the renovation of his son’s home had been halted for three weeks because several Amish workers got sick with measles.

Two childhood doses of the M.M.R. vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — can confer lifelong immunity.

The disease had been declared eliminated in the United States a quarter-century ago but has been resurgent amid declining vaccination rates.

Some families worry that the M.M.R. vaccine causes autism, though studies have repeatedly debunked that claim. And Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. secretary of health and human services, has sown doubts about the safety of vaccines.

David Leslein, a 33-year-old furniture maker who is Amish, said that his seven children were vaccinated against tetanus but had not received the M.M.R. vaccine because he feared they would be stricken by terrible side effects.

For years, many Amish children had religious exemptions to New York’s school immunization requirements, which require a slew of shots, including the M.M.R. vaccine.

But in 2019, schools emerged as a major locus of transmission during a measles outbreak in ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities. At the time, more than 26,000 students in the state had religious exemptions from being vaccinated.

Hoping to prevent future outbreaks, the state eliminated the exemptions. In doing that, New York became an outlier, with stricter school vaccination rules than those in 45 states.

Some Amish educators appear to have learned of the change two years later, when state health inspectors contacted them to inquire about their schools’ compliance, according to court documents.

When inspectors arrived at one schoolhouse, only one of 24 children had the required vaccination paperwork on file. Some of the children had paperwork indicating they had received some vaccines, but not others.

But Mr. Wengerd, who represents Amish and Mennonite schools in their interactions with state government, said that most Amish families he knew did not vaccinate their children for religious reasons, according to an affidavit he filed in court. He noted that the 26 families who sent children to the three schools had a total of 168 unvaccinated children.

“None of these 168 children have any diagnosed medical condition or any other health condition that arose or occurred after they were born,” he said.

The inspections led to hefty fines, as much as $2,000 per student, a huge sum for one-room schoolhouses that receive no public funding. By 2022, more than two dozen Amish and Mennonite parents had signed a declaration, beseeching the state to let them run their schools without interference.

“We, as a peace-loving religious group, are sincerely sorry that we are causing the state a prob.,” the handwritten declaration said. It explained that they cherished their religious freedom and the opportunity to raise children free of worldly influences. The vaccine requirement interfered with that. “If we honestly obey this, then it will affect everything we do, yes even in the way we try to remain healthy.”

The tone was humble, but firm. If pressed, the letter warned, Amish residents might leave. “We love our state of N.Y. + have no desire to move out,” the letter stated.

The letter did not sway the judge who was reviewing the Health Department’s evidence against the three schools, all located in Montgomery County, to the northwest of Albany. The fines, $118,000 in all, were upheld.

The Amish then sued in federal court, claiming that the Constitution entitled them to religious exemptions.

While declining to comment on the litigation, the state Health Department said in a statement that “New York’s school immunization requirements are based in science and protect the health and well-being of all New Yorkers.”

Federal courts have generally sided with public health arguments rather than with those citing individual liberty in vaccine cases, going back more than 100 years when smallpox remained a threat.

The Amish lost twice in federal courts, with a panel of appellate judges concluding that religious exemptions would result in “clusters of low vaccination rates.”

In December, the Supreme Court unexpectedly revived the case, instructing the lower courts to re-examine the Amish lawsuit in light of another recent ruling. That case, Mahmoud v. Taylor, was brought by parents who wanted to withdraw their children from public school classes when books with L.G.B.T.Q. themes were discussed. The Supreme Court concluded that requiring the children to participate in the lessons violated the parents’ rights to direct the religious upbringing of their children.

After suffering another adverse ruling in June, the Amish have now again asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

The Supreme Court accepts only a small fraction of appeals, but there is a much stronger chance it will take up this case, given its prior order, legal experts say.

Brad Hoylman-Sigal, the former state senator who led the effort to eliminate religious exemptions in 2019, said that the ongoing outbreak should give the Supreme Court pause. “It would be outrageous given the current state of emergency in New York for the Supreme Court to undo a health mandate that has effectively staved off measles outbreaks,” said Mr. Hoylman-Sigal, who is the Manhattan borough president.

A lawyer for the Amish, Hiram Sasser, said that the Supreme Court should not consider the current measles outbreak if it decides to take the case.

There is a strong constitutional tradition, he said, of exempting people from government mandates on the basis of religious beliefs.

Mr. Sasser is a lawyer at First Liberty Institute, which has a track record of winning religious liberty cases before the Supreme Court. He said that his goal was not to drive a hole through vaccine laws, but to get the court to order New York to leave the Amish alone.

“I don’t view this as a vaccine case,” he said. “I view this as a ‘Save the Amish’ case.”

If the Amish were to lose, he warned that some might depart in search of greater religious freedom elsewhere.

“We hope it won’t come to a wagon train fleeing New York, but if New York insists on these fines, and the Supreme Court does not grant them relief, that is likely the outcome,” he said.

Mark Sommer contributed reporting.
